title: Subversion of the Biopic with Maestro and Napoleon

commenti.body:
I don’t even think Maestro did a good job with the relationship between Bernstein and his wife. Or his children. Or his lovers. It’s just a movie that floats along, has some emotional moments, but in the end you’re kind of like “What was the point?”. What was being explored here?

I think Bradley Cooper wanted to make something different and more artsy, but ultimately didn’t really know how. So it’s just bits and pieces of various things that don’t really amplify and work together. It also drags a lot. It exhausted me and I almost fell asleep watching it even though it was the middle of the day.

Edit: I actually got physically exhausted thinking about this movie haha
He clearly wants an Oscar, that’s what he’s doing. It’s so painfully obvious a part of me just wants him to get it so he can stop trying 😂.

> It’s just a movie that floats along, has some emotional moments, but in the end you’re kind of like “What was the point?”. What was being explored here?

Yeah that seems to be said a lot but I think it was able to convey a lot. It showed a man struggling with his sexuality. It showed a man struggle with his image not only with the public but with his own children. It showed a wife who was fully and deeply in love with this complicated person regardless of his faults.

One of my favorite movies is Jacquot de Nantes directed by Agnes Varda and I was reminded of that movie a lot when watching Maestro. She made Jacquot as a love letter to her dying husband, Jaques Demy, with a movie about his own childhood. It is intercut with images of him in the present day dying of what everyone thought was cancer but was later revealed to be HIV. Art is hard. Loving an artist is hard. These figures we see in our head as perfect geniuses have faults too.
[deleted]

He wants to get all the traditional things that Hollywood gives out (the money, the fame, the accolades), but he also wants to be seen as a real artist. And so he ends up in this confusing middle ground.

Yeah I would say it's disingenuous to say he is only trying to get an Oscar. He obviously has a love of classic Hollywood and he also has a passion for composing. Maestro wasn't just some "sure maybe I'll win some awards" type movie. He wants to be taken seriously and I'm sure he would LOVE to win an Oscar but it's not the only reason he is doing these things.

It kind of only pays lip service to his struggles. It doesn’t go into them in much depth and that’s where the criticism about the movie not really giving you anything new about Bernstein comes from.

I almost feel like the intention was for it to be more about Felicia than Leonard. She’s the “maestro”, she’s the one conducting Leonard, she‘s the one struggling to mold his talent into whatever it’s supposed to be. It should be a movie about her artistic struggle and that’s why we get so little of Leonard’s.

I haven’t seen anyone coming away from the movie with that view and I think it’s because of the way the characters and the relationship is played.

Haven’t seen Napoleon, so I can’t really comment, but I think the best biopics (with the exception of Malcolm X) focus on a specific part of someone’s life that is their defining moment, rather than telling their cradle to grave story (Lawrence of Arabia, Moneyball, The Fighter, etc.). It’s far more interesting IMO as it avoids some of the tired paint-by-numbers scenes you get of a young T.E. Lawrence first seeing a picture of a camel in a book, or his eccentric grandparent telling him to travel the world or something like that. If I wanted to know why a historical figure was important or how they got into their field, I’d watch a documentary. Throw me straight in the thick of it please.

Because of this, I really liked Maestro. I appreciate why some people may want to see more of his impact, but I already know a fair bit about the work of Bernstein, so I’m glad they didn’t waste time spelling it out. I thought the exploration of the contradiction at the heart of Bernstein’s self-identity, his public persona and his relationship with Felicia made for a far better film.

I adore your analysis! I walked out of the cinema. It’s just so unfocused, treats the people he cheated with like props. Bernstein was an arrogant awful diva. By changing history you lose both cinematic and real life truth. I don’t want to be a broken record and tell the stories of the people I met in opera with Bernstein stories. The director doesn’t care about what really happened. You’re exactly right. The director wants to feel artsy. Make an artsy film. The result is trite. 

As for Napoleon, I’m going to trust the critics and avoid it. They say it’s his character as The Joker trying and failing to play Napoleon. An actor stuck in a character is a taxing chore. Getting stuck in a mindset or affectation makes subsequent films crummy. I was elated when I watched Dream Scenario. Nic Cage ditched affectation and just acted! For years he was stuck. Yeah watching Joaquin Phoenix stuck in an acting k hole isn’t my cup of tea.

Both of these movies failed in the same way (there are other flaws too).  They both take interesting subjects who complete amazing feats in their lives and they each largely avoid letting the audience enjoy in those accomplishments, which is a foundational story telling technique for engagement.

Independent of the ethics of his choices it would be fascinating to witness the rise of Napoleon and the subtle ways he outclassed his rivals. Weirdly, the movie largely avoids this and even the battles often lack emotional context.

Maestro pretty directly does the same thing. The movie starts with his big break (like Napoleon), and later does a significant time jump which avoids the audience seeing him become established professionally. 

I love movies that are character and relationship studies, but these two seem to avoid fun for no reason.

This is why I think Love and Mercy is a great biopic. It takes two vertical slices of the life of Brian Wilson, the first one being probably his peak in the Pet Sounds sessions and the last one being the later portion of his life just before his comeback with Love and Mercy. They’re both perfectly complementary and although it doesn’t cover his overall life, it’s pretty good giving the viewer a _reason_ to go out and search more about Brian Wilson, listen to his works and so on.

I too love the approach to Napoleon. As a young boy, I got disillusioned with the pro-Bonaparte propaganda my country likes to peddle from time to time and saw the man as a vainglorious piece of shit that brought misery upon the whole continent.
I was hoping Scott would perform a satirical takedown, and I was not disappointed. While the movie certainly did not lack gravity or grandeur in the portrayal of Napoleon, Phoenix and Scott set out to create a portrait of a pretty pathetic and emotionally unstable man who had a very hard relationship with his wife. Also, Napoleon's road in the movie is a classic fall arc: clinging to your delusions harder and harder as your whole life collapses in front of you. The movie's final shot is one of my favorites in a long time. Rivals Oppenheimer and the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

I do however hold against Scott the lack of emphasis on the Polish and Spanish threads in Napoleon's life of which there were plenty.

The problem with Maestro is that it centers its complete dramatic premise on the question whether or not his marriage will survive.  It's a flaw that exists on the script level.   Cooper's formal approach (as a director) is exemplary and the performances are top notch, but it's a telling of a tale that only those who know Bernstein's musical genius would appreciate and even then it still falls short.  The creative struggle to become the world's foremost conductor must also be a tangible obstacle in his journey and, paired with his relationship, the two arcs must create tension with one another.

" I love learning about the life of someone from another time and place and what made them tick."

I'm sorry, but I can't help but ask - Why not read a book?

Andrew Roberts' biography is spectacular. Informative as hell and a very entertaining read.

What's interesting is that I feel the opposite. I respect the subversion of the biopic tropes in Napoleon, but just couldn't get into Maestro.  It may have to do with your pre-existing knowledge of these figures.  I am a lot more familiar with Napoleon than I am Leonard Bernstein, so I appriciated the unique take on Napoleon's story. Whereas, I know very little about Leonard Bernstein so the focus on his relationships felt like it wasn't enough for me.

> but these two seem to avoid fun for no reason 

I saw an article talking about how good it was that Napoleon dispelled the “great man narrative”, by showing more of him being a cuckold. 

That his “masculine insecurity” with his wife’s cheating was more important to show than his accomplishments.

I audibly groaned. 🤦🏾‍♂️
I do also read.  I just happen to love movies too.

It’s a piece of art & entertainment, not a history textbook.  The “importance” of his accomplishments doesn’t matter a lick.   I don’t think the movie totally worked, but the satirical cuckold part was at least funny and a bit new.

> Haven’t seen Napoleon, so I can’t really comment, but I think the best biopics (with the exception of Malcolm X) focus on a specific part of someone’s life that is their defining moment, rather than telling their cradle to grave story (Lawrence of Arabia, Moneyball, The Fighter, etc.).

Agreed, especially when it comes to someone like Napoleon. His life was so eventful it'd warrant a multi-season HBO series, almost impossible to cover all the important bits in a film that's just a couple of hours long.

If that was his goal I don't think the movie worked at all based off reviews I've seen .


Also the movie did lack gravity and grandeur honestly I'm tired of historically inaccurate films on real ppl . Napoleon real life is lot more interesting than that mess of a film .
